newsitem.title: UK: Copper games continue despite Hamanaka exit.
newsitem.headline: Copper games continue despite Hamanaka exit.

text.p: Current activity in the copper market, with stocks at low levels and a high backwardation but an unresponsive price, puzzles many who feel that 10 years of mystery moves ended with the exit of Yasuo Hamanaka.

London Metal Exchange (LME) inventories on Tuesday fell 4,225 tonnes to 109,175 tonnes, the lowest since August 1990. But price movement was modest, suggesting that traders are wary of headline falls in stocks.
"It is very hard to make sense of this. It looks like somebody is trying to keep it in a range," a senior trader said.

"Traders continue to smell a rat and remain very wary about putting too much trust into the LME stock erosion. For a start, post the Sumitomo Corp debacle traders are aware that copper has been living a lie for many years, so why not a few more months," an analyst said.

In June Sumitomo fired former head trader Hamanaka after it alleged that he admitted running up losses now put at $2.6 billion in 10 years of unauthorised trading. Hamanaka has since been arrested and was charged on Tuesday with fraud.
The market remains unpredictable, as, since September 1996, there has been a 166,600-tonne or 60 percent fall in LME stocks, mostly out of European and U.S. warehouses.
The overall global stocks/weeks consumption ratio has fallen as well, and is under four weeks - a critical level.
But LME prices have largely been rangebound, barring short-lived spikes, at either just below $1,900 and just above $2,000. By midday Tuesday, prices were trading around $2,040.

Many traders continue to feel the drawdowns in stocks reflect arbitrage opportunities that arose in the autumn, with premiums sucking metal towards China or from LME U.S. warehouses into American Comex stores.

Much of the metal may end up either in bonded warehouses in China and available for re-export or it may be parked in Singapore and then put back onto LME warrant. There has also been talk in recent weeks of sizeable tonnages of perhaps 40,000 tonnes being landed in Singapore awaiting warranting, but this has not yet transpired. And some said on Tuesday that around 15,000 tonnes of unwarranted copper will move out soon to the Middle East for consumption.

On Tuesday only 100 tonnes were registered, taking the Singapore total to just 2,750 tonnes, what it was in September. However, removing copper out the system may also be designed to keep prices within a range, as the residue of Sumitomo's old unauthorised market positions are unwound.
Some traders said a U.S. investment house has taken stock off the LME to maintain prices in order to prevent downside put option positions inherited from Sumitomo being exercised.
Others said this manoeuvre, which also involved a European trader, was also designed to squeeze out the major short in the market.
"It is very odd, what with all the regulatory attention on copper now," one said.
Because of the headline falls in stocks, the LME backwardation, which was erased earlier this year, has flared out to near $80 at present.
"I would not be surprised to see the backwardation go out to $100...This is a game for big boys with big chequebooks and risk appetites," the senior trader said.

The eventual outcome of current phantom falls in stocks will be harmful for the copper market in the longer term, as supply/demand surpluses grow year-on-year towards the end of the century, fundamental analysts said.
"Assuming this copper is being harboured, not consumed, then at some stage it will be put back on warrant," Nick Moore of the Flemings Global Mining Group said.
Copper supplies will surge in 1997, and current high prices will only encourage miners to speed up expansions.

"By the end of this millenium we expect a surplus in excess of 1.2 million tonnes...Prices will have to move down to the cost of production which is $0.60/0.65 a lb ($1,323/ 1,433 per tonne)," Moore said.
